I find **five repeats, three different main claims, and four ambiguous pairs**. None of the incoming records explicitly says it revises, confirms, or denies the stored statement.

The distinction matters in cases such as V12: both records mention $89 billion of data-center revenue, but one’s main claim is total company revenue and the other’s is the data-center business and its customer mix. The labels below describe what the supplied sources report; they do not establish whether those reports are true.

1. **V01 — Repeats; high confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Nvidia announced a $12.9 billion deal to buy Hugging Face. The Augusta Free Press article says: “On Thursday, NVIDIA … announced a $12.9 billion deal to purchase Hugging Face.”  
   **Incoming:** Nvidia announced a $13 billion Hugging Face acquisition. IndexBox says: “announced on Thursday its acquisition … for $13 billion.”  
   The parties, transaction and Thursday announcement match; $13 billion is consistent with rounding $12.9 billion. The incoming report cites EU Tech Loop and Euronews. Neither passage establishes completion.

2. **V02 — Ambiguous; medium confidence.**  
   **Stored:** On September 2, Cramer cited $9.26 earnings per share for “this year” and over $15 for “next year.” His words are: “$9.26 earnings estimate for this year” and “over $15 a share next year.”  
   **Incoming:** Fool.com cites analyst consensus of $9.26 for **fiscal 2027** and $15.59 for **fiscal 2028**: “fiscal 2027 earnings of $9.26 per share” and “fiscal 2028 earnings estimate of $15.59 per share.”  
   The figures are compatible, but Cramer does not name fiscal years or identify the source of his estimates. His “this year” and “next year” should not automatically be equated with the incoming record’s fiscal years, nor should his cited estimates automatically be attributed to the same consensus.

3. **V03 — Repeats; high confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Nebius’s Q2 revenue grew 454% year over year, with more computing capacity coming online. Fool.com says: “revenue skyrocketed 454% year over year” and attributes it primarily to “more computing capacity coming online.”  
   **Incoming:** Nebius’s second-quarter revenue grew 454% year over year, described as organic and demand-driven. The other Fool.com article says: “revenue grew by 454% year over year” and “it was organic growth.”  
   The same author reports the same company, quarter and growth figure on September 5 and 6. The explanations add detail; the sources do not present them as mutually exclusive.

4. **V04 — Repeats; high confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Nvidia agreed in August to guarantee up to $105 billion for an Ohio data center with Nvidia systems leased to OpenAI for 20 years. Fool.com says: “guarantees of up to $105 billion for a data center project in Ohio” and “20-year leases to OpenAI.”  
   **Incoming:** The same August guarantee and lease arrangement. BigGo says: “guarantees of up to $105 billion for a data center project in Ohio” and “20-year leases to OpenAI.”  
   The August 2026 date is inferred from the September 2026 publication dates. These are reports of an agreement, not proof that the guarantee was paid or the project completed.

5. **V05 — Ambiguous; medium confidence.**  
   **Stored:** AWS plans to deploy **another** 2 million Nvidia GPUs **in calendar 2027 and 2028**. Fool.com says: “another 2 million Nvidia GPUs in calendar years 2027 and 2028.”  
   **Incoming:** AWS and Nvidia announced a target of 2 million GPUs **by 2028**. FXLeaders says: “targeting the deployment of 2 million NVIDIA GPUs across AWS infrastructure by 2028.”  
   These may describe the same collaboration, but the incoming article does not say the 2 million are additional, and “by 2028” does not establish the same deployment window. It reports a joint target; the stored article describes an AWS plan.

6. **V06 — Different; high confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Supplier commitments rose from $119 billion to $279 billion, with the $160 billion increase primarily due to memory procurement. Fool.com says: “increased its commitments to suppliers to $279 billion, up from $119 billion” and attributes the increase to memory procurement in Kress’s prepared statement.  
   **Incoming:** Total future spending commitments were $366 billion, including $279 billion for supply and capacity. The other Fool.com article says: “$366 billion in future spending commitments, including $279 billion related to supply and capacity.”  
   The $279 billion component overlaps, but the incoming record’s main claim is the **larger total**, not the increase or its cause. The incoming article’s “latest quarter” is identifiable as fiscal Q2 2027 from its discussion of results.

7. **V07 — Ambiguous; medium confidence.**  
   **Stored:** AWS plans another 2 million Nvidia GPUs in calendar 2027 and 2028: “another 2 million Nvidia GPUs in calendar years 2027 and 2028.”  
   **Incoming:** AWS is deploying another 2 million GPUs “through Q2 FY2029,” according to BigGo.  
   The company, incremental quantity and subject strongly suggest a connection, but the stated end points differ: fiscal Q2 2029 is not simply calendar year-end 2028. The incoming sentence also does not itself specify Nvidia GPUs. Neither article explicitly connects or reconciles the schedules.

8. **V08 — Repeats, with an unresolved date discrepancy; medium confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Nvidia announced a $13 billion Hugging Face acquisition. IndexBox says: “announced on Thursday its acquisition … for $13 billion.”  
   **Incoming:** Nvidia announced an agreement to acquire Hugging Face for $11.9 billion cash plus $1 billion in options. Calcalistech says: “Over the weekend, Nvidia announced … $11.9 billion in cash and another $1 billion in options.”  
   The same buyer, target and approximately $12.9 billion consideration point to the same acquisition; the incoming record adds the consideration breakdown. But “Thursday” and “over the weekend” do not match as announcement dates in these September 6 reports. I would preserve that discrepancy rather than silently choose a date.

9. **V09 — Different; high confidence.**  
   **Stored:** Nvidia agreed to an up-to-$105 billion guarantee for an Ohio data-center project with 20-year OpenAI leases. Fool.com says: “guarantees of up to $105 billion for a data center project in Ohio.”  
   **Incoming:** Nvidia had guaranteed up to **$108.5 billion in total**, including $105 billion for an OpenAI data-center project. The other Fool.com article says: “guaranteed up to $108.5 billion, including a $105 billion guarantee.”  
   The $105 billion project is shared, but the incoming record’s main claim is the broader guarantee total. Its sentence does not explicitly date that total: the preceding sentence dates **spending commitments** to quarter-end, so the record’s quarter-end date for guarantees is not clearly established by the quoted text.

10. **V10 — Repeats; high confidence.**  
    **Stored:** Nvidia expects about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, with supply constraints limiting the forecast relative to demand. Fool.com reports Huang: “revenue to grow about 70% in its fiscal 2028” and says the forecast is constrained by component supply.  
    **Incoming:** Management expects 70% growth in the next fiscal year. Another Fool.com article says Kress reported that “management expects 70% revenue growth in the next fiscal year.”  
    Both describe Nvidia management’s forecast, not separate analyst estimates. The reporting attributes it to different executives; the incoming article does not name the fiscal year in that sentence, but its Q2 context and the stored article’s fiscal calendar support the same next fiscal year. The supply qualification is absent from the incoming record.

11. **V11 — Repeats; high confidence.**  
    **Stored:** Nvidia’s supplier commitments increased from $119 billion to $279 billion; Kress attributed the $160 billion increase primarily to memory procurement. Fool.com says: “$279 billion, up from $119 billion” and “primarily due to memory procurement.”  
    **Incoming:** Nvidia exited fiscal Q2 with $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments, up from $119 billion, with scheduled amounts by fiscal year. BigGo says: “$279 billion of supply and capacity commitments, up sequentially from $119 billion.”  
    The same company, quarter and two amounts identify the main claim. The incoming record adds the schedule; it does not repeat Kress’s explanation. The sources use “supplier” versus “supply and capacity” commitments, so that wording difference should remain visible.

12. **V12 — Different; high confidence.**  
    **Stored:** Nvidia’s fiscal Q2 2027 **total revenue** was $96.2 billion, up 106%, including $89 billion in data-center sales. Fool.com says: “revenue soared by 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, including $89 billion” from data centers.  
    **Incoming:** A later quarter’s **data-center revenue** was $89 billion, beating an $85.8 billion forecast; hyperscale and ACIE growth are also reported. Yahoo’s article says: “Data Center revenue reached $89 billion” and “ACIE revenue surged 138%.”  
    The $89 billion component overlaps, but the incoming main claim concerns the segment’s performance and mix, not the stored record’s total-company result. The incoming article says “a later quarter” after its first-quarter discussion; it does not explicitly name fiscal Q2 2027 in that passage, so the quarter match remains an inference.

**结论：最强的选项，是把现在“一次三选一”的 Jev 比较，拆成两个各只问一件事的问题。** 一个问“是不是同一件事”，一个问“有没有明确改变”。每个候选各问一遍，再由代码按现有 `outcome()` 组合。这是假设，不是已证事实。

先说明三件事：

- **计划文件**：Write 工具被禁用，没法创建计划文件，所以内容都在这条回复里。
- **挑战轮**：本次是只读规划，我没有跑新的 Codex–Claude 挑战轮。我读了已有的独立 Codex 报告 `reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/codex-independent.md`，它的方向和我的追踪一致。所以这不是两份独立证据，发送前必须再跑挑战轮。
- **本次操作**：没有调用任何模型，没有改任何文件，没有碰运行中的数据库。

打个比方：现在的 Jev 像一个考官，要在三个格子里选一个。“重复”和“修订”其实各由两个事实拼成，是不是同一件事，以及有没有改变。两件事缠在一起时，概率就被撕成 0.48 对 0.46。

## 我自己追踪的案例

| 案例 | 搜索 / 比较 / 记录映射 | 原始数字和来源 | 已确认 vs 线索 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **H01** 漏合并 20→8 | 搜索找到了，`8:E1` 是第 1 个候选（`poc/data/clean-acceptance-2026-11-09/step2/decisions.json:5356`）。是比较失败。 | different 0.57 / same 0.41（`:5368-5375`）。探针 Jev single 三次是 0.59/0.37。 | 两条文字里有 $12.9bn 和 $13bn，而 `same_statement` 条款已写“precision may differ”（`clean-arch/step2/compare.py:58-59`）。DeepSeek 三次判 same，所以文字本身够判断。两位盲读者都判 same。 |
| **B06** 假修订 30→20 | 级联：20 没并进 8，成了独立组。 | `30:e1` 对 `8:E1`（同为 12.9）是 same 0.87（`:11317-11323`）。对 `20:ev-1`（$13bn）是 supersedes 0.67（`:11309-11316`）。 | 线索：“数字不一样”的读法同时造成一次漏合并和一条假修订。只有 2 对，机制没有证明。 |
| **B05** 假修订 | 搜索找到，比较错。 | `9:e5` supersedes 0.48 / different 0.46（`decisions.json:4515-4521`）。探针 full 0.51/0.48/0.46，single 三次 different。 | 两位读者都判 different。新记录文字里没有“受供应限制”，旧记录有，但这是否是原因未证明。 |
| **B10** 假合并 | 搜索找到，比较错。记录边界有问题。 | same 0.49 / different 0.36。探针 full 是 0.45，随后两次判 different。 | 旧记录 `13:e4` 把“已在生产”和“占收入 20%”捆在一条里（`library.json:2352`）。摘要写 Nvidia said，引文却是记者口吻。“主陈述”本身就含糊。 |
| **R05** 有争议 | 高分：supersedes 0.86–0.88，两种臂都是。 | 旧记录自己写“we'll update this story if we hear back”（`r05-adjudication-blind.json:32`）。新文章里 Nvidia 既不确认也不否认。 | 旧记录的 `original_party` 写成 Nvidia，但停产说法其实来自报道。线索：这可能触发了“同一说话人修订”条款，只是推测。读者意见分裂，保持争议。 |
| **P01** | 目标边对（0.99）。额外边 `45:e3` 约 0.88。 | `45:e3` 是捆绑的 NVL576 说法。 | 额外边有争议，不能算对也不能算错。 |

整体模式来自 `decisions.json`：明显不同的候选几乎都是 1.0/0.0，错误多数落在被撕开的区间。但这个区间里也有读者认可的合法合并（0.47、0.41、0.41、0.49，见 `reports/step2-merge-fix-council-2026-11-09/stored-census.md:16`）。而 R05 的 0.88 和云厂商/开发者那条 0.84 是高分错误。所以分数既不能当门槛，也不能当解释。

另有一条没验证的线索：同一篇文章的记录彼此看不见（`compare.py:13-14`）。B05 的 70% 说法同时命中 `14:e2`（0.90）、`9:e3`（0.70）、`9:e1`（0.61），可能已经散成几个组。

数量线索来自 `reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/repeat-trace-leads.json`，只是映射，没读原文。冻结参照里 55 个后续重复成员，34 条映射干净且有更早的组。其中 25 条并进去了，9 条没有，9 条里有 8 条更早的组在候选里。H01 是这 9 条之一。这不是漏合并率。

## 备选方案对比

| 方案 | 状态 | 为什么不够 |
|---|---|---|
| 概率门槛 | 已证不够 | 只挡 1/4 错合并，同时挡 4 条被接受的和 1 条重叠。H01 找不回，高分错误挡不住。 |
| J2“没有新信息才算重复” | 已证否 | 合并从 102 降到 22，合法转述一起被拆（`clean-arch/step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md:155-159`）。 |
| 独立模型 DeepSeek | 已测，线停了 | H01、R05 好，但 B05 三次全错。它只有单对标签，没有组排名，模型、格式、提供商同时变。 |
| 加数字 / 整篇文章 | 与现有决定冲突 | PRD §5、§14 刻意把 `figures` 排除在比较之外。整篇文章没被点名排除，但 B05 旧文章并排写了 70% 和翻倍，全文会让 Jev 把兄弟说法当主陈述。 |
| 检索分数给 Jev | 利弊未证 | 试验六例后中断。 |
| 只加“材料不足”出口 | 假设 | `src/hivemind/views/jev_matching.py:30` 的主题关系有 `cannot_tell`，片段问题没有。但怎么处理“不确定”是 Alex 的产品决定。 |
| 代码里比较数字 / 传递一致 | 未证 | 比较数字要用被排除的 `figures`。传递规则对“同于 B 又修订 A”的合法情形会误伤。 |
| 只改展示 | — | 找不回 H01，也修不了 B05。 |

只有拆分能让每个候选同时得到“是否同一件事”和“有没有改变”。这样漏合并和每一条修订边都能逐条回放。搜索没找回的候选它覆盖不了，线索里只有 1 条。

## 拆分的内容和风险

- **来源**：不是新标准。两个问题的每一句都来自 `compare.py:58-65` 的 `PIECES`，也就是 PRD §5 表和 D168 的定义。Jev 在 clean 路径里已经用过 `noul` 是/否问题（`compare.py:73-93`），不需要新能力。
- **问题一**：新记录是否报告旧记录的主陈述，允许转述、精度和新增细节不同。
- **问题二**：新记录是否是主陈述的后来版本且有改变，包括同一说话人修订、官方确认或否认。“没有改变也没有确认否认”这半句是唯一新增字，需要提示审计。
- **组合**：沿用 `THRESHOLD = 0.5`（`jev_matching.py:17`）和 `outcome()`（`compare.py:109-118`），不新增门槛。同一候选两个问题都≥0.5 时，只记下分歧，不写入。
- **最大风险**：它可能只是把三选一重新贴了标签。B05 的“主陈述是否同一条”这个难点还在问题一里，照样可能给 0.48。D202 有先例：把“确认/否认”单独分出来，挡住 4 条错的，却影响了 3 条对的修订（`docs/DECISIONS-log.md:2596`），当时没采用。D201 还发现，提示臂之间的差异在一次抽样噪声内。所以拆分是否有用，只能靠实验判断。

## 下一步：一个推荐，分两段

**段一：不花钱，先做。** 问题是：存档里的失败，是比较文字不够，还是比较错了。

1. 取六个案例的全部候选边，加上那 9 条没并进去的线索和 25 条并进去的对照，再加 D392 d1 的 56 条 supersedes 里按固定种子选的一批。
2. 交给两位没看过 Jev 答案的读者，也不能在同一个包里看到答案选项。上一轮读者就看到了（`RESULTS-DRAFT.md:30`）。
3. 分两种读法：只看 Jev 当时的比较文字，再看完整原文。分别记录决定性事实是否在比较文字里。
4. 读之前先写下哪些算“搜索”、“比较”、“记录映射”。H01 必须被归为“找到但没并”。
5. 推翻条件：如果只看比较文字时两位读者就互相不同意，失败属于输入或记录边界，拆分救不了。此时停下，把边界问题报告给 Alex。
6. 还必须找到至少一条两位读者都认可的真正“后来改变”的修订。目前没有（`COUNCIL-LOOP.md:43`）。找不到，实验就不能声称保护了合法修订。

**段二：同输入小实验，需要 Alex 同意。** 同一天发原版 Jev 完整批次（对照）、原版 Jev 单对、拆分版完整批次，每个案例三次。案例是 H01、B06、B05、B10、R05、P01（含 `45:e3`）、B01，加段一选出的对照。按真实 `outcome()` 回放每条候选，先报回退再报改善。

费用是估计，不是账单。完整请求约 8.7k 输入 token，拆分后约两倍，按仓库价 $0.042/M 输入，15 个案例三次约 $0.05。仓库的保守预留公式会更高。按 AGENTS §9，超过几美分要 Alex 同意，上次的“开始”只覆盖那一次。

发送前要做完整请求的提示审计，并跑 Codex 加 Claude 的挑战轮。还要先写下推翻条件：

- H01 没被找回，即三次里至少两次问题一 <0.5。
- 任何合法重复对照在拆分版里三次中至少两次不再是重复，而原版保持。
- B05 或 R05 的错误边仍在三次中至少两次出现。
- 撕开的案例拆开后没有比原版更远离 0.5。
- 同一对三次之间不一致的情况不少于原版。

任何一条成立就停，不再调提示。

小样本只能杀死假设，或证明值得更大的测试，不能给出准确率、召回率或产品收益。三次抽样也不保证相互独立。

## 需要 Alex 决定的事

1. 是否开新的 Step 2 比较版本来测拆分。现在的比较是冻结配置，改动只能由他开。
2. 段二的花费。
3. 采用之前才需要：两个问题都为真、或被撕开的对子，怎么处理，是新组、重复还是待定。
4. R05 的边界：同一出版方更谨慎的跟进，算不算“原始来源修订”。
5. 捆绑记录（B10、P01 额外边）属于 Step 1，本范围内只报告，不处理。

## 限制

- 所有“读者意见”都是 AI 读者，不是冻结金标。
- 25 + 9 条线索我没逐条读原文，数字只是映射线索。

## 5. Step 2: find and compare related evidence

### Why this is separate

An open thesis may accumulate many evidence records. Step 1 needs to understand the article and the open research; it does not need to read every prior statement to do that. Step 2 uses each proposed `{thesis, evidence}` association to find the history worth comparing.

### Find candidate evidence

The proposed design places semantic search over the evidence library. It uses the thesis and incoming evidence to find top-N related evidence across the current entity, including evidence linked to other theses. The thesis is search context, not a restriction to evidence already linked to that thesis. This also applies when the proposed thesis is new. For example, “raised its revenue outlook” and “expects higher sales” can be related despite different wording. Alex chose this entity-wide scope on 2026-11-06.

Search returns **candidates**, not a final decision. Alex discussed a starting point of top 10; the implementation and quality requirements need to be measured.

A match outside the returned set will not be considered by the comparison. Search quality therefore matters independently from the model's ability to compare the records it receives.

### Compare with Jev

**2026-11-08 (candidate, [round log](step1-unfiled-2026-11-08/LOG.md) §§24, 31–35):**
- Comparison reads the full passages; the 600-character cut is removed.
- An unlinked record also searches by its own text.
- `figures` never enter a search or comparison text.
- Jev is asked the clean path's own piece question, aligned with line 2's test: a repeat reports the stored piece's main statement, and
  an official's denial of a report is a revision.
- When a thesis opens, every stored unlinked group from earlier articles is judged against it in batches of ten (a yes/no question; the
  company's overall results inform only a revenue or earnings thesis). Each judged pair is recorded once.
- On c6's records: search 97.9%, wrong merges 1.9% (2 of 104), both lines met; line 3 not re-measured.

Jev compares the new evidence with the returned evidence. The intended outcomes are:

| Outcome | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Repeat | The new material presents the same statement again. | Another article reports the same company forecast. |
| Revision | A later account changes the same statement. | The company revises its forecast from 12% to 25%. |
| New evidence | It is not identified as a repeat or revision of the evidence compared. | A different analyst offers a separate forecast. |

The words, amount, speaker, source and time can matter to the comparison. A later statement about the same subject is not necessarily a revision. A matching amount alone does not prove that two statements are the same.

The result “new evidence” is the outcome of the comparison performed; it is not proof that no matching evidence exists elsewhere in the library. When the incoming evidence is judged a repeat of several candidates, it joins only the group Jev judges it most like: the highest same-statement probability, with ties going to the earliest group (Alex, 2026-11-08). A comparison that fails is not saved and is reported.

**Repeat handoff:** when Jev identifies a repeat, the comparison must retain the identity of the existing evidence record it was compared against. Step 3 uses that identity to place the incoming record in the existing record's group, adding its source and any missing thesis link. The typed Jev response need not generate the record ID: the caller can associate the choice with the candidate it supplied. The rule for several matching candidates is stated above.

**Step 2 acceptance (Alex, 2026-11-08).** Three lines apply:
1. For incoming evidence whose earlier version is in the library, search returns it at least 90% of the time.
2. At most 2% of merges are clearly wrong.
3. Grouped dossiers keep no fewer details added by later reports than no merging does.

The first measurement against these lines is in the [Step 2 log](step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md) §12; the isolated modules are `step2/compare.py` and `step3/library.py`.

The diagram's intended sequence is: use `{thesis, incoming evidence}` to search the evidence library; pass the returned candidates and incoming evidence to Jev; pass the comparison result and the proposed association to Step 3. For a new thesis, search the same entity-wide evidence library. A concrete working draft of the Jev comparison request appears in [section 13](#13-step-2-prompt-jev-working-draft).

## 6. Step 3: save evidence and links

Step 3 takes the proposals from Step 1 and the comparison outcomes from Step 2 and writes the resulting research information.

| Result | What is saved |
|---|---|
| New thesis with supporting evidence | The new thesis and its evidence link; save new evidence or reuse a matching record according to Step 2. |
| New evidence for an existing thesis | The evidence and its link to the thesis. |
| Repeat | Place the incoming record in the existing evidence record's group: add its source and any missing link to the relevant thesis, and keep the incoming record's own text and fields inside the group. Do not rewrite the existing record, and do not create a separate evidence record for the same statement. |
| Revision | The new evidence and its source, linked to the earlier statement as a revision. |

A revision does not erase the earlier statement. On 2026-11-06, Alex chose to keep one evidence record for a repeat and add the new source and any missing thesis link. On 2026-11-08 the Step 2 validation showed that keeping only the earlier text discards details a later report adds, such as a guidance condition; Alex then chose to keep each repeat's own text and source inside the stored record's group, without rewriting the original ("A 继续；跑council loop 开始做"; [Step 2 log](step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md) §7). How a judgement reads a group is being tested. Multiple articles reporting the same statement do not automatically establish independent original sources. The current production writer stores separate repeat records, so this is a change for the clean path and needs implementation and verification; the existing historical records remain available. Step 3 ends when the chosen thesis, evidence and relationships are saved. How they are physically stored and written is a separate implementation decision.

reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:173:        "text": "Nvidia's Net Income Could Top $850 Billion by 2029, Eclipsing Aramco's Record\nNvidia could generate approximately $851 billion in annual net income by fiscal 2029 if Wall Street's 64% compounded EPS growth forecast holds, a figure that would eclipse Saudi Aramco's record $161.1 billion annual profit by more than fivefold and rival Switzerland's GDP. The projection is grounded in reported results: Q2 FY2027 revenue of $96.22 billion, up 106% year over year, with a $2 trillion cloud backlog and projected hyperscaler capex of $1.3 trillion in 2027. CEO Jensen Huang said the entire supply chain is running flat out, with the company carrying $279 billion in supply commitments. The growth outlook faces a potential headwind from the Federal Reserve, where markets price a 60% chance of a rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting amid an unusually intense pressure campaign from the Trump administration to cut rates instead.\nNvidia's profit trajectory has reached a scale that defies conventional corporate comparison. If Wall Street's compounded earnings growth projections materialize, the chipmaker could report annual net income of roughly $851 billion by fiscal 2029 -- a figure that would not only shatter the all-time corporate profit record but would also rival the entire economic output of Switzerland.\nThe projection, derived from a 64% compounded EPS growth rate applied to a trailing-12-month base of approximately $193 billion in net income and $7.91 in diluted EPS, stands in stark contrast to the current record holder. Saudi Aramco posted $161.1 billion in annual profit in 2022, a number that Nvidia's projected Year 3 earnings would eclipse more than fivefold.\nThe stepwise path is ambitious by any standard. Year 1 EPS of $13.0 would translate to about $316 billion in net income, followed by $21.3 (about $519 billion) in Year 2, and $34.9 (about $851 billion) in Year 3. Backing into revenue at Nvidia's current profitability profile suggests Year 3 sales would land near $1.35 trillion -- roughly four to 4.5 times the trailing-12-month revenue of about $303 billion.\nThe foundation is grounded in reported results rather than speculation. Nvidia's most recent quarter, Q2 FY2027 reported August 26, delivered $96.22 billion in revenue, up 105.85% year over year, with net income of $59.688 billion, up 125.9%. Full-year FY2026 net income was $120.067 billion, up from just $4.368 billion in fiscal 2023.\nThe argument for such extraordinary growth rests on a demand picture that management describes as effectively insatiable. Data Center revenue reached $89.023 billion in Q2, up 117% year over year. The company is selling more components of the overall AI system -- CPUs, GPUs, NVLink, and networking products -- which means it benefits not only from more data centers being built, but from generating more revenue per gigawatt of capacity deployed.\nCustomer commitments back the ramp. AWS is deploying an additional 2 million GPUs through Q2 FY2029. OpenAI has committed to approximately 12 gigawatts of Nvidia compute through 2030. Neocloud partners are expected to exit the year with eight gigawatts of installed capacity, up from about three gigawatts at the end of 2025.\nJensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, was blunt about the supply constraints. \"Our entire supply chain is challenged. CFO Colette Kress noted that customer forecasts currently indicate revenue may double next year. Of that total, $92 billion is scheduled for the rest of fiscal 2027, $87 billion for fiscal 2028, and $88 billion for fiscal 2029.\nThe extraordinary growth projections arrive amid an intensifying political battle over monetary policy that could directly affect the AI buildout's financing costs. Ten days before the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting, the Trump administration has mounted an unusually broad public pressure campaign against a potential rate hike.\nPresident Donald Trump escalated the pressure Friday by threatening to halt trade with countries that run trade surpluses with the U.S. unless the Fed cuts interest rates -- a direct linkage he had never before made. \"In the old days... if we announced good [economic] numbers, interest rates went down. Officials point to the three-month annualized CPI rate of 1.6% as evidence that inflation is contained.\nFed officials see a different picture. The three-month annualized core PCE rate -- the Fed's preferred gauge -- is running at just over 3%. Three Fed officials dissented at the July meeting in favor of a quarter-point hike: Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his Jackson Hole speech that 54% of the 199 components in the PCE price measure had risen more than 3% over the previous 12 months.\nMarkets are pricing in roughly 60% probability of a rate hike at the September meeting, bolstered by a strong jobs report on Friday. The meeting comes just two months before November midterm elections in which polls show widespread voter dissatisfaction with higher prices and interest rates.\nThe inflationary dynamics are not solely about Trump's policies. The AI infrastructure buildout itself is creating a textbook supply-demand mismatch. Demand for AI hardware vastly outstrips supply, giving infrastructure providers extraordinary pricing power. The FOMC has noted that these higher prices are working their way down to consumers.\nFor Nvidia investors, the $851 billion projection reframes the debate entirely. Fiscal 2028 EPS estimates have moved from $12.60 ninety days ago to $15.40, with 52 analysts covering the fiscal year and zero downward revisions in the trailing 30 days. The breakdown is 95 bullish to 2 bearish. Q3 FY27 revenue is guided to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, excluding China Data Center compute.\nCapital return remains active. Nvidia returned about $26.0 billion to shareholders in Q2, with $99.0 billion remaining under the buyback authorization. If Vera Rubin ramps as promised and hyperscaler capex holds, the record book for corporate profitability may indeed need a new binding."

reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:346:        "text": "Nvidia is no longer just an AI chip company. It is financing the revolution it built\nNvidia has expanded from GPUs into networking, software, computing systems and strategic investments in AI companies, while helping finance the infrastructure that buys its products. With revenue expected to approach $400 billion this year, investors are asking how long the extraordinary growth can continue.\nNvidia’s numbers have long since transcended the boundaries of a typical chip company. The company is expanding from processors into communications, software, computing systems and investments in AI companies, while also helping to finance the ecosystem that buys its products. In doing so, it is becoming not just the major supplier of the AI revolution, but one of the companies shaping and funding it.\nA week and a half ago, Nvidia published its second-quarter results for fiscal 2027. Nvidia reports according to a fiscal year that does not coincide with the calendar year, with its fiscal year ending in the last week of January. The company’s revenue totaled $96.2 billion, an increase of 106% from the corresponding quarter, and it expects revenue of about $108 billion in the next quarter. The results and forecast reinforced expectations that rapid growth will continue through calendar 2027. Following the earnings report, Nvidia’s stock soared, and on August 27, the company’s market value reached about $5.5 trillion. The following day, the stock experienced a slight sell-off, and its market value fell to $5.24 trillion.\nNvidia is the company with the greatest impact on the AI revolution. The processors, computing systems, networking equipment and software it develops form much of the infrastructure on which many of the world’s most advanced AI models are built and run. In recent years, the company has rapidly expanded its product and service offering, from GPU chips to processors, communications systems, storage, software and complete computing systems, with the aim of becoming a central provider of almost every layer of data center infrastructure required for the AI era. Some of that expansion has been achieved through acquisitions.\nNvidia’s success raises a broader question: Is this an unusual investment cycle, or the beginning of a long-term structural change in the semiconductor industry?\nNvidia is the world’s most valuable company and the clear leader in the semiconductor sector. Traditionally, the sector has been cyclical, with periods of rapid growth in demand and investment alternating with periods of overcapacity, inventory buildup and slowdown. A common rule of thumb is a three- to five-year cycle, although the length varies widely across different segments of the industry.\nThe cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry is particularly evident in the memory chip market, but it also exists in processors, CPUs and other areas. However, the expansion of demand for GPUs and AI systems is taking place on a different scale. Huge investments by cloud companies and data centers in AI infrastructure are rapidly increasing demand for computing and may extend the positive investment cycle beyond the traditional cyclicality of the chip industry. As a result, investors in the semiconductor sector are constantly looking for signs that the growth rate is beginning to change.\nThe performance of the capital markets illustrates how unusual the current cycle is. The SOXX basket fund, which invests in semiconductor stocks, rose about tenfold from the end of June 2019 to the end of June 2026, compared with a 2.5-fold increase in the SPY basket fund, which tracks the S&P 500. Nvidia’s stock itself rose about 48-fold over the same period. Part of the extraordinary increase is also related to the acquisition of Mellanox, completed in 2020, which significantly expanded Nvidia’s activities in communications and networking for data centers.\nSince the beginning of July this year, the SOXX basket fund has retreated by about 20%. Nvidia, on the other hand, returned to a price close to the peak it recorded earlier this year following its strong earnings report. The gap between Nvidia’s performance and that of the broader sector illustrates that investors do not value all chip companies in the same way, and that Nvidia continues to benefit from exceptionally high growth expectations.\nNvidia employs approximately 42,000 people worldwide, including about 6,000 in Israel. Its Israeli operations have expanded rapidly since the acquisition of Mellanox and include a significant presence in communications, chips, software and systems engineering. Because of its size and scope, Nvidia has a growing impact on the Israeli economy, including exports, employment, activity in the high-tech industry and state tax revenues.\nOver the past decade and into the beginning of this decade, Nvidia has significantly upgraded its GPU chips. Products that once focused primarily on graphics processing have become central parallel processors for artificial intelligence applications, simulations and data centers.\nIn 2022, Nvidia introduced the Hopper GPU architecture, led by the H100 processor. The product family is primarily designed for training and running large AI models, high-performance computing and data centers.\nIn 2024, Nvidia launched its Blackwell architecture, expanding the company’s approach from a single processor to a complete system that includes a CPU, GPU, memory, communication between accelerators and software.\nIn December 2025, Nvidia acquired a significant portion of Groq’s technology, particularly its LPU architecture, which was designed specifically for inference, running already-trained models and generating responses at high speed. The deal included a payment of $13 billion and an additional $4 billion in future payments.\nAnother leap forward is the Vera Rubin architecture. Its main innovation is the closer integration of processors, AI chips, memory and communications, allowing large systems to operate faster and more efficiently. Vera Rubin is designed not only for training models but also for optimizing inference, producing more responses in less time and with lower power consumption, particularly for large models. During the analyst call following the earnings release, Nvidia said that systems based on Vera Rubin had already been delivered commercially to customers during August 2026.\nOver the weekend, Nvidia announced that it had agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $11.9 billion in cash and another $1 billion in options. Hugging Face will bring Nvidia models, a developer community and runtime capabilities. Together with the Groq deal, the acquisitions expand Nvidia’s product and service offering into additional parts of the AI chain, as the company seeks to increase the sources of revenue it generates from each data center.\nThe expectation is that the mix of data center workloads will gradually change, shifting from a high proportion of training, the process of developing models, performed mainly by companies building large language models, toward a growing share of inference, or running already-trained models to generate answers, perform tasks and power AI-based applications.\nNvidia’s preparation for this shift is evident in the combination of Groq technology, which specializes in fast, low-latency inference, and the Vera Rubin platform, which can integrate Groq 3 LPX accelerators dedicated to inference alongside Vera Rubin’s GPU and CPU.\nInvestors’ concern stems from the expectation that Nvidia will face more intense competition in chips designed for inference, particularly from Google. A shift in the mix of data center workloads toward inference could therefore create a greater competitive challenge for Nvidia.\n92% of revenue comes from data center infrastructure\nThe AI revolution has enabled Nvidia to deliver an extraordinary increase in revenue. In fiscal 2023, which ended in January 2023, the company’s revenue totaled $26.97 billion. In fiscal 2024, it jumped to $60.92 billion, and in fiscal 2025, it doubled again to $130.5 billion. In fiscal 2026, which ended in January 2026, the growth rate moderated to 65%, while revenue reached $215.9 billion.\nThis year, however, revenue is expected to jump to about $400 billion, an increase of about 85% from the previous year. During the analyst call, Nvidia said it expects revenue to increase by another 70% next year, with that fiscal year ending in January 2028. The company’s confidence in the forecast stems, among other things, from its assessment that demand will remain high and that the factor limiting sales will be chip supply and production capacity.\nNvidia’s gross margin was about 75% in each of the first two quarters. It is expected to fall to about 74% in the third quarter and 71%-72% in the fourth quarter, mainly because of the sharp increase in memory chip prices. The operating margin was about 66% in the first two quarters, and its expected decline later this year is expected to be more moderate than that of the gross margin, thanks to the sharp increase in revenue and the fixed component of operating expenses.\nBased on these assumptions, the company’s operating income this year is expected to be approximately $260 billion, while net income on a non-GAAP basis is expected to reach approximately $218 billion.\nIn this analysis, it is preferable to use non-GAAP data, partly because of the company’s conservative approach to neutralizing certain accounting expenses and because these figures exclude capital gains from investments, which were significant this year. Nvidia reported investment gains of $15.94 billion in the first quarter and $7.77 billion in the second quarter. As noted, these gains are excluded from our analysis.\nApproximately 92% of Nvidia’s revenue comes from data center infrastructure, including chips and connectivity. In the first half of the year, the company’s three largest direct customers accounted for 44% of revenue. Geographically, about 62.4% of revenue came from customers headquartered in the United States. Since these are companies with multinational operations, some of those sales ultimately went to other regions. About 28% of revenue came from Taiwan, about 8% from China and Hong Kong, with China’s direct share accounting for less than 1%, and 1.6% from the rest of the world.\nNvidia’s expected earnings multiple for this year is about 24, based on a market value of $5.24 trillion and estimated non-GAAP net income of $218 billion. However, the company’s revenue and earnings are expected to continue growing rapidly next year. According to the assumptions in this analysis, based on revenue growth of about 70% and a gross margin of about 72%, revenue could reach approximately $680 billion and net income about $370 billion. That would bring the forward earnings multiple down to about 14, which appears low relative to the expected growth rate.\nUnder these assumptions, Nvidia’s stock does not look expensive based on its forward earnings multiple relative to its expected growth rate. This conclusion is also supported by the relatively high probability that the company will meet its sales target for next year. If demand for data center infrastructure continues to grow rapidly from 2028 onward and Nvidia manages to maintain its leading position, further growth in revenue and profits could support a further increase in the share price.\nThe negative scenario, however, includes a slowdown in the construction of new data centers beginning toward the end of the current decade, the emergence of significant competition from other companies, and the accelerated development of dedicated AI chips by Nvidia’s largest customers themselves. These factors could slow the growth of revenue and profits and weigh on the share price.\nAnother risk is rapid improvement in computing efficiency. If more AI functionality can be extracted from each unit of hardware, the growth rate in demand for chips could be lower than the growth rate in AI usage.\nNvidia divides its data center revenue into two main markets: hyperscale customers, which mainly include cloud providers and large internet companies, and the rest of the market, defined as ACIE, AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise.\nNvidia makes this analytical distinction to show the sources of growth in its data center business and illustrate the expansion of demand beyond the relatively limited group of hyperscale customers. A broader distribution of demand could reduce Nvidia’s dependence on hyperscale customers, which are themselves exposed to the risk of developing dedicated chips, as well as to changes in the composition of demand as the AI market gradually shifts from model training toward inference.\nIn the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia’s revenue from hyperscale customers reached $48.7 billion, an increase of 13% from the previous quarter. ACIE revenue totaled $40.3 billion, an increase of 25%.\nAccording to Nvidia’s forecast, most of the growth in the third quarter is expected to come from ACIE, while growth in hyperscale is expected to accelerate again in the fourth quarter and throughout fiscal 2028 as the supply of the Vera Rubin platform expands. As noted, Nvidia expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow by about 70%, with supply constraints expected to remain a limiting factor at least through the end of that year.\nAlongside its business expansion, Nvidia has significantly increased its investment activity across the AI ecosystem. The company reported that, as of the end of the quarter, it had about $99 billion invested in shares of other companies, as well as another $25 billion in commitments for future investments. These investments are focused on AI model makers, infrastructure companies and other private companies.\nThe investments help fast-growing companies finance the computing and data center infrastructure they need, allowing Nvidia to bridge the gap between the large investments those companies require and the future cash flow expected to result from them. But this also raises concerns about potential circular financing: Nvidia invests in companies that can then use that money to purchase Nvidia infrastructure and processors.\nNvidia, on the other hand, argues that these are also strategic investments in companies with the potential to become technology leaders, strengthening the ecosystem and supporting long-term demand for accelerated computing.\nOne of Nvidia’s most notable investments was in xAI, Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, which was later merged into SpaceX. Following the merger, Nvidia held 122.8 million SpaceX shares at the end of June, now worth about $17 billion. Another significant investment is in Intel. At the end of June, Nvidia held 214.8 million Intel shares worth about $20 billion. In both cases, Nvidia benefited from a significant increase in the value of its holdings.\nIn August 2026, Nvidia entered into memoranda of understanding with six major investment and financial institutions to establish independent financing platforms designed to raise more than $500 billion from third parties over time to build AI infrastructure. The move is intended to facilitate financing for the acquisition of Nvidia products.\nWill demand for AI grow fast enough?\nNvidia expects a significant decline in gross margin over the next two quarters, mainly because of the sharp increase in component costs, particularly memory prices. As noted, the gross margin was 75% in the second quarter, and Nvidia expects it to decline later this year. In fiscal 2028, the gross margin is expected to stabilize at around 72%-73%, after the price increases take effect in the first quarter.\nThe advanced memory market is largely dominated by three manufacturers: SK Hynix and Samsung of South Korea, and Micron of the United States. Of particular importance is HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, which has become a vital component in advanced AI computing systems and one of the key growth drivers of the memory market. Demand for HBM is expected to continue growing rapidly in 2027, with shipments expected to increase by approximately 50%-60%, although still not enough to meet full demand.\nHowever, part of the increase in memory manufacturers’ revenue and profitability also stems from a sharp rise in component prices caused by supply constraints. This creates a risk for the shares of the three memory manufacturers. If they increase production capacity faster than expected, if additional manufacturers enter the market, or if the growth rate of AI demand moderates, the balance of power in the market could change.\nIn such a scenario, a decline in memory prices could lead to a sharp drop in the profitability of memory manufacturers and, consequently, weigh on their share prices. On the other hand, at least over the next two years, the current pricing environment could allow memory manufacturers to report exceptionally high profitability.\nThe conclusion is that the AI revolution is expected to change the intensity and length of the investment cycle in the semiconductor industry, but it will not eliminate the cycle itself.\nNvidia is in a unique position. It is benefiting from the rapid expansion of demand for accelerated computing, expanding its share of the data center value chain and trying to ensure that its massive investments across the AI infrastructure ecosystem will continue to generate demand for its products even as the center of gravity shifts from training to inference.\nThe key question is whether demand for AI will grow fast enough to justify the massive investments currently being made in AI infrastructure. Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary of that spending, but it is also increasingly dependent on the future development of the very market it is helping to build.\nThe writer is an economist at an Israel-based tech company."
reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:369:        "text": "Historically, September has been a difficult month for Wall Street. The S&P 500 has fallen by an average of about 1.1% during the month from 1926 through 2024. Yet Nvidia ( NVDA +2.55% ) stock has gained ground in seven of the past 10 Septembers, with a median return of about 1.5%. Hence, while the September Effect may offer a reason for some caution around the overall stock market, it hasn't been such a negative indicator for Nvidia's stock.\nAnd recently, CEO Jensen Huang also gave investors a potentially more important signal. He said Nvidia expects revenue to grow about 70% in its fiscal 2028, which begins Jan 31, 2027. But management says even that forecast doesn't reflect the full scope of demand for its offerings; it's constrained by the limited supply of components required to build its artificial intelligence (AI) platforms.\nNvidia's visibility into future demand is sharpening\nIn its fiscal 2027 second quarter (which ended July 26), Nvidia's revenue soared by 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, including $89 billion in sales from the data center segment. However, management's long-term outlook was even more impressive.\nWall Street analysts had previous expected the company to deliver fiscal 2028 revenue of about $570 billion, translating to growth of roughly 44%. Nvidia's guidance, however, implies revenue of close to $700 billion.\nCEO Jensen Huang said that Nvidia has never offered revenue guidance for a full year in advance before. However, this time, the company has much better visibility into memory and manufacturing capacity, as well as the land, power, and data-center infrastructure needed to deploy its products. Some of this infrastructure needs to be secured two to three years in advance.\nSupply constraints could limit Nvidia's fiscal 2028 growth\nCFO Colette Kress highlighted that customer forecasts currently indicate Nvidia's revenue may double next year. Huang also said Nvidia's revenue growth could be \"a lot higher\" if the company were not supply-constrained.\nNvidia exited the fiscal second quarter with $279 billion of supply and capacity commitments, up sequentially from $119 billion. These commitments are primarily related to memory purchases and manufacturing capacity. Of that total, $92 billion is scheduled for the rest of fiscal 2027, $87 billion for fiscal 2028, and $88 billion for fiscal 2029.\nNvidia's largest customers are also continuing to spend heavily on AI infrastructure. Amazon ( AMZN +0.56% ) Web Services plans to deploy another 2 million Nvidia GPUs in calendar years 2027 and 2028. Nvidia also expects the combined capital expenditures of the top five hyperscalers to approach $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.\nThe demand trends look impressive, even when the company is not factoring any data center compute revenue from China into its current outlook. Hence, a meaningful recovery of its position in the Chinese market is not currently part of Nvidia's growth expectations.\nNvidia's revenue opportunity per AI data center is expanding\nNvidia is also expanding its revenue opportunity from each gigawatt (power capacity) of AI infrastructure. Management estimates that this opportunity has increased from roughly $18 billion with Hopper GPUs to $25 billion with Blackwell systems and $40 billion with Vera Rubin systems. These increases are partly a result of the fact that Nvidia is selling more components of the overall AI system, including CPUs, GPUs, NVLink (Nvidia's high-speed technology for connecting GPUs and other processors), and other networking products. Hence, the company benefits not only from the construction of more AI data centers, but also because it is generating more revenue per gigawatt of new capacity deployed.\nIncreasing adoption of agentic AI could further drive demand for compute capacity. Huang said AI agents can require roughly 15 to 100 times more compute than direct human use of AI, depending on the task. These agents can also run continuously and interact with other agents. Hence, future demand for Nvidia's wares may increasingly depend on the actual use of AI applications rather than on the computing power required to train AI models.\nNvidia's growth outlook also comes with risks\nNvidia, however, has warned that customer demand forecasts can prove inaccurate. Its customers may also delay purchases because of constraints related to data center infrastructure or capital availability. In such a scenario, Nvidia's large commitments to its own suppliers could result in higher costs.\nNvidia is also providing support for some large AI infrastructure projects. In August, the company agreed to provide guarantees of up to $105 billion for a data center project in Ohio. That campus will exclusively host Nvidia computing systems under 20-year leases to OpenAI . Huang also said AI labs for which Nvidia expects to use its balance sheet could account for roughly one-quarter of the company's business in fiscal 2028.\nRising memory costs could also pressure profitability. Nvidia expects its gross margins to fall from 75% in the fiscal second quarter to around 71% to 72% in the fiscal fourth quarter, before improving to around 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028. Management attributed much of this pressure to sharp increases in memory prices.\nNvidia's stock also faces near-term pressure. On Sept. 1, rising Treasury yields and oil prices pushed the Nasdaq Composite down by 1%. Besides these marketwide risks, Nvidia is also facing concerns about some of its AI financing arrangements. Its stock slipped by 1.5% during the session.\nSeptember could still bring volatility for Nvidia investors. However, it is obvious that Nvidia now has much greater visibility into demand several years ahead. If that visibility holds, short-term weaknesses could matter far less than the scale of the growth opportunity the company is preparing for.\nBy Manali Pradhan, CFA – Sep 5, 2026 at 4:54AM EST\nNvidia has increased its supply and capacity commitments from $119 billion to $279 billion as it prepares for future AI infrastructure demand.\nNvidia's revenue opportunity per gigawatt could rise from about $18 billion with Hopper GPUs to $40 billion with Vera Rubin systems."

reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:475:        "text": "Nvidia's Net Income Could Top $850 Billion by 2029, Eclipsing Aramco's Record\nNvidia could generate approximately $851 billion in annual net income by fiscal 2029 if Wall Street's 64% compounded EPS growth forecast holds, a figure that would eclipse Saudi Aramco's record $161.1 billion annual profit by more than fivefold and rival Switzerland's GDP. The projection is grounded in reported results: Q2 FY2027 revenue of $96.22 billion, up 106% year over year, with a $2 trillion cloud backlog and projected hyperscaler capex of $1.3 trillion in 2027. CEO Jensen Huang said the entire supply chain is running flat out, with the company carrying $279 billion in supply commitments. The growth outlook faces a potential headwind from the Federal Reserve, where markets price a 60% chance of a rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting amid an unusually intense pressure campaign from the Trump administration to cut rates instead.\nNvidia's profit trajectory has reached a scale that defies conventional corporate comparison. If Wall Street's compounded earnings growth projections materialize, the chipmaker could report annual net income of roughly $851 billion by fiscal 2029 -- a figure that would not only shatter the all-time corporate profit record but would also rival the entire economic output of Switzerland.\nThe projection, derived from a 64% compounded EPS growth rate applied to a trailing-12-month base of approximately $193 billion in net income and $7.91 in diluted EPS, stands in stark contrast to the current record holder. Saudi Aramco posted $161.1 billion in annual profit in 2022, a number that Nvidia's projected Year 3 earnings would eclipse more than fivefold.\nThe stepwise path is ambitious by any standard. Year 1 EPS of $13.0 would translate to about $316 billion in net income, followed by $21.3 (about $519 billion) in Year 2, and $34.9 (about $851 billion) in Year 3. Backing into revenue at Nvidia's current profitability profile suggests Year 3 sales would land near $1.35 trillion -- roughly four to 4.5 times the trailing-12-month revenue of about $303 billion.\nThe foundation is grounded in reported results rather than speculation. Nvidia's most recent quarter, Q2 FY2027 reported August 26, delivered $96.22 billion in revenue, up 105.85% year over year, with net income of $59.688 billion, up 125.9%. Operating margin ran 60.38%, net margin 55.6%, and return on equity hit 101.5%. Full-year FY2026 net income was $120.067 billion, up from just $4.368 billion in fiscal 2023.\nThe argument for such extraordinary growth rests on a demand picture that management describes as effectively insatiable. Data Center revenue reached $89.023 billion in Q2, up 117% year over year. The cloud industry backlog now exceeds $2 trillion, according to management, with top-five hyperscaler capital expenditures projected at nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.\nNvidia's revenue opportunity per gigawatt of AI infrastructure has stepped up dramatically across product generations: from roughly $18 billion on Hopper to $25 billion on Blackwell to $40 billion on Vera Rubin. The company is selling more components of the overall AI system -- CPUs, GPUs, NVLink, and networking products -- which means it benefits not only from more data centers being built, but from generating more revenue per gigawatt of capacity deployed.\nCustomer commitments back the ramp. AWS is deploying an additional 2 million GPUs through Q2 FY2029. OpenAI has committed to approximately 12 gigawatts of Nvidia compute through 2030. Neocloud partners are expected to exit the year with eight gigawatts of installed capacity, up from about three gigawatts at the end of 2025.\nJensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, was blunt about the supply constraints. \"Our entire supply chain is challenged. And everybody is really running flat out,\" he said. The company guided fiscal 2028 revenue growth to approximately 70% year over year -- a forecast that management says still doesn't reflect the full scope of demand. CFO Colette Kress noted that customer forecasts currently indicate revenue may double next year. Huang added that growth could be \"a lot higher\" if the company were not supply-constrained.\nNvidia exited the fiscal second quarter with $279 billion of supply and capacity commitments, up sequentially from $119 billion. Of that total, $92 billion is scheduled for the rest of fiscal 2027, $87 billion for fiscal 2028, and $88 billion for fiscal 2029.\nThe extraordinary growth projections arrive amid an intensifying political battle over monetary policy that could directly affect the AI buildout's financing costs. Ten days before the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting, the Trump administration has mounted an unusually broad public pressure campaign against a potential rate hike.\nPresident Donald Trump escalated the pressure Friday by threatening to halt trade with countries that run trade surpluses with the U.S. unless the Fed cuts interest rates -- a direct linkage he had never before made. \"In the old days... if we announced good [economic] numbers, interest rates went down. Now, if you announce good numbers, interest rates go up because they're so afraid of inflation,\" Trump told reporters.\nSenior economic counselor Peter Navarro called members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee \"clowns\" in an interview with former Trump advisor Steve Bannon, warning that a rate hike would be \"careless\" and \"would hit precisely the sectors America needs to prosper most.\" Vice President JD Vance said, \"We believe that the Fed should be lowering interest rates,\" while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued the Fed typically doesn't raise rates during a supply shock until there are second- or third-order inflationary effects.\nThe administration's core argument is that growth itself does not cause inflation, and that supply-side expansion through tax cuts and capital investment expands the economy's capacity to grow without generating price pressure. Officials point to the three-month annualized CPI rate of 1.6% as evidence that inflation is contained.\nFed officials see a different picture. The three-month annualized core PCE rate -- the Fed's preferred gauge -- is running at just over 3%. Three Fed officials dissented at the July meeting in favor of a quarter-point hike: Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his Jackson Hole speech that 54% of the 199 components in the PCE price measure had risen more than 3% over the previous 12 months.\nMarkets are pricing in roughly 60% probability of a rate hike at the September meeting, bolstered by a strong jobs report on Friday. The meeting comes just two months before November midterm elections in which polls show widespread voter dissatisfaction with higher prices and interest rates.\nThe inflationary dynamics are not solely about Trump's policies. reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:498:        "text": "Historically, September has been a difficult month for Wall Street. The S&P 500 has fallen by an average of about 1.1% during the month from 1926 through 2024. Yet Nvidia ( NVDA +2.55% ) stock has gained ground in seven of the past 10 Septembers, with a median return of about 1.5%. Hence, while the September Effect may offer a reason for some caution around the overall stock market, it hasn't been such a negative indicator for Nvidia's stock.\nAnd recently, CEO Jensen Huang also gave investors a potentially more important signal. He said Nvidia expects revenue to grow about 70% in its fiscal 2028, which begins Jan 31, 2027. But management says even that forecast doesn't reflect the full scope of demand for its offerings; it's constrained by the limited supply of components required to build its artificial intelligence (AI) platforms.\nNvidia's visibility into future demand is sharpening\nIn its fiscal 2027 second quarter (which ended July 26), Nvidia's revenue soared by 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, including $89 billion in sales from the data center segment. However, management's long-term outlook was even more impressive.\nWall Street analysts had previous expected the company to deliver fiscal 2028 revenue of about $570 billion, translating to growth of roughly 44%. Nvidia's guidance, however, implies revenue of close to $700 billion.\nCEO Jensen Huang said that Nvidia has never offered revenue guidance for a full year in advance before. However, this time, the company has much better visibility into memory and manufacturing capacity, as well as the land, power, and data-center infrastructure needed to deploy its products. Some of this infrastructure needs to be secured two to three years in advance.\nSupply constraints could limit Nvidia's fiscal 2028 growth\nCFO Colette Kress highlighted that customer forecasts currently indicate Nvidia's revenue may double next year. Huang also said Nvidia's revenue growth could be \"a lot higher\" if the company were not supply-constrained.\nNvidia exited the fiscal second quarter with $279 billion of supply and capacity commitments, up sequentially from $119 billion. These commitments are primarily related to memory purchases and manufacturing capacity. Of that total, $92 billion is scheduled for the rest of fiscal 2027, $87 billion for fiscal 2028, and $88 billion for fiscal 2029.\nNvidia's largest customers are also continuing to spend heavily on AI infrastructure. Amazon ( AMZN +0.56% ) Web Services plans to deploy another 2 million Nvidia GPUs in calendar years 2027 and 2028. Nvidia also expects the combined capital expenditures of the top five hyperscalers to approach $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.\nThe demand trends look impressive, even when the company is not factoring any data center compute revenue from China into its current outlook. Hence, a meaningful recovery of its position in the Chinese market is not currently part of Nvidia's growth expectations.\nNvidia's revenue opportunity per AI data center is expanding\nNvidia is also expanding its revenue opportunity from each gigawatt (power capacity) of AI infrastructure. Management estimates that this opportunity has increased from roughly $18 billion with Hopper GPUs to $25 billion with Blackwell systems and $40 billion with Vera Rubin systems. These increases are partly a result of the fact that Nvidia is selling more components of the overall AI system, including CPUs, GPUs, NVLink (Nvidia's high-speed technology for connecting GPUs and other processors), and other networking products. Hence, the company benefits not only from the construction of more AI data centers, but also because it is generating more revenue per gigawatt of new capacity deployed.\nIncreasing adoption of agentic AI could further drive demand for compute capacity. Huang said AI agents can require roughly 15 to 100 times more compute than direct human use of AI, depending on the task. These agents can also run continuously and interact with other agents. Hence, future demand for Nvidia's wares may increasingly depend on the actual use of AI applications rather than on the computing power required to train AI models.\nNvidia's growth outlook also comes with risks\nNvidia, however, has warned that customer demand forecasts can prove inaccurate. Its customers may also delay purchases because of constraints related to data center infrastructure or capital availability. In such a scenario, Nvidia's large commitments to its own suppliers could result in higher costs.\nNvidia is also providing support for some large AI infrastructure projects. In August, the company agreed to provide guarantees of up to $105 billion for a data center project in Ohio. That campus will exclusively host Nvidia computing systems under 20-year leases to OpenAI . Huang also said AI labs for which Nvidia expects to use its balance sheet could account for roughly one-quarter of the company's business in fiscal 2028.\nRising memory costs could also pressure profitability. Nvidia expects its gross margins to fall from 75% in the fiscal second quarter to around 71% to 72% in the fiscal fourth quarter, before improving to around 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028. Management attributed much of this pressure to sharp increases in memory prices.\nNvidia's stock also faces near-term pressure. On Sept. 1, rising Treasury yields and oil prices pushed the Nasdaq Composite down by 1%. Besides these marketwide risks, Nvidia is also facing concerns about some of its AI financing arrangements. Its stock slipped by 1.5% during the session.\nSeptember could still bring volatility for Nvidia investors. However, it is obvious that Nvidia now has much greater visibility into demand several years ahead. If that visibility holds, short-term weaknesses could matter far less than the scale of the growth opportunity the company is preparing for.\nBy Manali Pradhan, CFA – Sep 5, 2026 at 4:54AM EST\nNvidia has increased its supply and capacity commitments from $119 billion to $279 billion as it prepares for future AI infrastructure demand.\nNvidia's revenue opportunity per gigawatt could rise from about $18 billion with Hopper GPUs to $40 billion with Vera Rubin systems."

reports/step2-jev-strengthening-council-2026-11-09/blind-12-packet.json:519:        "text": "NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) biggest lingering investor concern was customer concentration, CNBC reported. Nvidia relies on hyperscalers Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, along with major buyers Meta and SpaceX, for an outsized share of revenue, and in May began splitting its data center reporting into \"hyperscalers\" versus everyone else, a group it calls AI clouds, industrial, and enterprise, or ACIE. In the first quarter, the two segments were nearly even, at $37.9 billion for hyperscalers and $37.5 billion for ACIE, with ACIE growing 31% versus a slower pace for hyperscalers. CEO Jensen Huang has said the \"easiest go-to-market\" is hyperscalers \"because there are only five or six of them,\" versus \"250,000 companies\" in the broader industry Nvidia hopes to reach.\nNVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA )'s actual results answered the concentration question better than investors feared. In a later quarter, Data Center revenue reached $89 billion (beating the $85.8 billion forecast), while CFO Colette Kress noted that hyperscale revenue more than doubled. ACIE revenue surged 138%, an outcome showing the smaller, more diversified customer base is now growing even faster than the concentrated hyperscaler group Nvidia has leaned on most heavily.\nHuang's own framing shows the concentration is a go-to-market choice, not a structural ceiling. Huang has described hyperscalers as simply the \"easiest\" customers to sell to first because there are only a handful of them, while pointing to roughly 250,000 other companies as the long-term addressable market. It means today's concentration shows where Nvidia started selling, not the limit of where it can sell.\nEven Nvidia's most concentrated customers keep buying at scale despite their own cost pressures. Hyperscalers have continued purchasing GPUs in bulk even as their free cash flow gets squeezed by capital spending, evidence that AI infrastructure remains a top spending priority for these companies rather than an area facing near-term cutbacks.\nThe underlying dependence is still there, even if this quarter's mix improved. Nvidia continues to draw an outsized share of revenue from just three hyperscalers plus Meta and SpaceX. Each of those companies is actively designing its own custom chips specifically to reduce reliance on Nvidia. It is a long-term competitive threat that one strong ACIE quarter does not eliminate.\nHyperscaler customers are under financial strain from the same AI buildout that benefits Nvidia. Hyperscalers are seeing their free cash flow erased by the capital expenditures funding their GPU purchases, and if that financial pressure eventually forces any of them to slow spending, Nvidia's largest revenue source would be directly exposed regardless of how fast the smaller ACIE segment is growing.\nNVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) also has yet to prove that it can rapidly turn its much larger enterprise opportunity into comparable revenue. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC that recent financing announcements had produced \"a lot of headlines and big numbers and not a lot of details on how this stuff is going to work yet.\" It means the strategy to convert 250,000 potential customers into revenue remains more promise than proof.\nInsider Monkey's database shows NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) was held by 285 hedge funds in the second quarter of 2026, up from 275 in the first quarter, with total holdings valued at $94.67 billion. AMD, the chipmaker most often cited as Nvidia's closest rival, was held by 164 funds, up from 134, with holdings worth $23.58 billion.\nNvidia's growing ACIE business gives investors a clearer diversification story, but its biggest customers still drive most of its sales. If Nvidia expands to smaller clients while tech giants keep spending heavily on AI, it can lower its risk without slowing down growth. However, in-house custom chips and sudden budget cuts from giant buyers could still trigger sharp demand drops."

def outcome(answers, order):
    """answers: {group id: {'choice', 'probabilities'}}; order: group ids in creation order."""
    same = [g for g, a in answers.items() if a['choice'] == 'same_statement']
    later = [g for g, a in answers.items() if a['choice'] == 'supersedes']
    if same:
        best = max(same, key=lambda g: (answers[g]['probabilities']['same_statement'], -order.index(g)))
        return {'kind': 'repeat', 'repeat_of': [best], 'revises': later}
    if later:
        return {'kind': 'revision', 'revises': later}
    return {'kind': 'new'}



### Why this is separate

An open thesis may accumulate many evidence records. Step 1 needs to understand the article and the open research; it does not need to read every prior statement to do that. Step 2 uses each proposed `{thesis, evidence}` association to find the history worth comparing.

### Find candidate evidence

The proposed design places semantic search over the evidence library. It uses the thesis and incoming evidence to find top-N related evidence across the current entity, including evidence linked to other theses. The thesis is search context, not a restriction to evidence already linked to that thesis. This also applies when the proposed thesis is new. For example, “raised its revenue outlook” and “expects higher sales” can be related despite different wording. Alex chose this entity-wide scope on 2026-11-06.

Search returns **candidates**, not a final decision. Alex discussed a starting point of top 10; the implementation and quality requirements need to be measured.

A match outside the returned set will not be considered by the comparison. Search quality therefore matters independently from the model's ability to compare the records it receives.

### Compare with Jev

**2026-11-08 (candidate, [round log](step1-unfiled-2026-11-08/LOG.md) §§24, 31–35):**
- Comparison reads the full passages; the 600-character cut is removed.
- An unlinked record also searches by its own text.
- `figures` never enter a search or comparison text.
- Jev is asked the clean path's own piece question, aligned with line 2's test: a repeat reports the stored piece's main statement, and
  an official's denial of a report is a revision.
- When a thesis opens, every stored unlinked group from earlier articles is judged against it in batches of ten (a yes/no question; the
  company's overall results inform only a revenue or earnings thesis). Each judged pair is recorded once.
- On c6's records: search 97.9%, wrong merges 1.9% (2 of 104), both lines met; line 3 not re-measured.

Jev compares the new evidence with the returned evidence. The intended outcomes are:

| Outcome | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Repeat | The new material presents the same statement again. | Another article reports the same company forecast. |
| Revision | A later account changes the same statement. | The company revises its forecast from 12% to 25%. |
| New evidence | It is not identified as a repeat or revision of the evidence compared. | A different analyst offers a separate forecast. |

The words, amount, speaker, source and time can matter to the comparison. A later statement about the same subject is not necessarily a revision. A matching amount alone does not prove that two statements are the same.

The result “new evidence” is the outcome of the comparison performed; it is not proof that no matching evidence exists elsewhere in the library. When the incoming evidence is judged a repeat of several candidates, it joins only the group Jev judges it most like: the highest same-statement probability, with ties going to the earliest group (Alex, 2026-11-08). A comparison that fails is not saved and is reported.

**Repeat handoff:** when Jev identifies a repeat, the comparison must retain the identity of the existing evidence record it was compared against. Step 3 uses that identity to place the incoming record in the existing record's group, adding its source and any missing thesis link. The typed Jev response need not generate the record ID: the caller can associate the choice with the candidate it supplied. The rule for several matching candidates is stated above.

**Step 2 acceptance (Alex, 2026-11-08).** Three lines apply:
1. For incoming evidence whose earlier version is in the library, search returns it at least 90% of the time.
2. At most 2% of merges are clearly wrong.
3. Grouped dossiers keep no fewer details added by later reports than no merging does.

The first measurement against these lines is in the [Step 2 log](step2-validation-2026-11-07/LOG.md) §12; the isolated modules are `step2/compare.py` and `step3/library.py`.

The diagram's intended sequence is: use `{thesis, incoming evidence}` to search the evidence library; pass the returned candidates and incoming evidence to Jev; pass the comparison result and the proposed association to Step 3. For a new thesis, search the same entity-wide evidence library. A concrete working draft of the Jev comparison request appears in [section 13](#13-step-2-prompt-jev-working-draft).

## 6. Step 3: save evidence and links

Step 3 takes the proposals from Step 1 and the comparison outcomes from Step 2 and writes the resulting research information.

# Frozen-member trace: investigative leads, not a score

Alex asked how to strengthen Jev. Previous council recommended checking the frozen source-reference repeat members before choosing a fix. The reference `poc/data/clean-acceptance-2026-11-09/settled.json` has 26 groups and 55 later members marked repeat (plus one revision). These are article-level research matters, not Step 2 records. The reference and all historical outputs remain unchanged.

`repeat_trace.py` reads the two saved independent article-to-item reader outputs A and B by exact matter ID. It retains a provisional mapping only if both say kept and name the same single item; a matter appearing in more than one frozen group or an item assigned to multiple matters is explicitly excluded as a bundled/multiple mapping. It does not use textual substring matching to identify the case. It then traces the actual recorded candidate groups and final placement. This is a mechanical lead generator, not a semantic scorer or a replacement for source-backed review. H01 known positive control confirms that reference `20:ev-1` searched earlier `8:E1`, Jev chose different and the saved outcome was new.

| Preliminary mapping state for 55 later members | Count |
|---|---:|
| Both reader maps agree on one item, no marked multiple-matter/group mapping | 37 |
| A reader's matter judgment missing | 4 |
| Matter/item occurs across multiple matters or reference groups | 11 |
| Readers disagree or another status | 2 |
| Both readers call the matter missed | 1 |

For the 37 agreement mappings, 25 have an earlier reference group's ID among candidates and are placed in one of those groups; 8 have a candidate but are not placed in any prior mapped group; 1 has no corresponding prior group in its candidates; and 3 have no earlier eligible mapped record. This is **not missed-repeat recall, precision or a Jev error count**. Two readers assigning matter IDs to the same record does not prove the two full records have the same main statement, especially when one quotes several facts. Earlier source group originals, not later members, are what Jev actually compares. The 8 are high-priority trace leads; some clearly feature a different main claim, attribution or period, so cannot all be counted as a defect. All original prior/current record IDs, historical candidate group IDs, outcome and reader mapping states are preserved in `repeat-trace-leads.json`. The 55-reference population is conditional on the reference and 11-member story concentration; no global sample inference is warranted.

**Examples of why the underlying definition matters:** H01 (`20:ev-1 → 8:E1`) is the independently source-read missed repeat of a $12.9bn / rounded $13bn acquisition announcement. `14:e2 → 9:e1` is the independently source-read 70% company guidance, while the reports name different executives. In `13:e9 → 9:e13`, the newer record leads with $108.5bn total guarantees, including a $105bn Ohio guarantee, while the earlier record centers on the $105bn Ohio guarantee itself; the source-level matter cluster alone does not settle whether these full records are the same statement. In `24:e8 → 9:e7`, the 2m AWS GPUs have different reported period wording (through fiscal Q2 2029 vs calendar 2027–28), and that difference must be resolved against sources before calling a miss. These show why raw counts cannot be turned into a threshold or case-specific rule.

Next: manually read every lead against both complete articles and the actual Jev input; keep source-reference ambiguity and source/period attribution explicit. Review a sample of the 25 seemingly joined cases to ensure matching was meaningful. The approach and all claims must be independently checked before any model prompt or code changes.
